  Vision-language-action models are typically built on a simple premise: perception is first compressed by visual encoders, and action reasoning begins only afterwards. Yet manipulation often hinges on precisely the visual signals most vulnerable to this abstraction, e.g., local geometry, boundaries, depth, and subtle state changes. This raises a fundamental question: should action policies inherit a fixed visual endpoint, or directly access evolving visual computation? We introduce NEO-VLA, a structurally encoder-free vision-language-action framework. Images are tokenized by lightweight patch convolutional layers and evolve jointly with language throughout the backbone, allowing a flow-matching action expert to draw from instruction-conditioned visual representations at different depths. This simple change reveals a consistent pattern. Native architectures outperform encoder-based counterparts under controlled comparisons; full fine-tuning reduces but does not erase the gap, and additional scale alone cannot recover it. More strikingly, layer-wise probing shows that the action-critical signals often peak well before the final visual representation. Across diverse manipulation settings and distribution shifts, NEO-VLA consequently achieves stronger and more robust control. Together, these results suggest that embodied control benefits from access to visual representations across the computational hierarchy, rather than a fixed encoder output.
  </details>

- **[Route First, See Later: Enabling Vision Agents to Reason Scientifically by Separating Routing Policy from Action Spaces](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.06760)**  `arXiv:2611.06760`  
  _Shubhabrata Mukherjee, Jeffrey Donatelli, Daniela Ushizima_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Scientific image-analysis workflows require agents to select among diverse capabilities like description, detection, counting, and segmentation. Current multi-tool architectures conflate intent interpretation with visual execution, masking whether a failure arises from flawed reasoning (misrouting) or failed perception (invalid tool execution). This lack of auditability renders agents unreliable for high-stakes scientific automation. We introduce ZETA, an extensible architecture that operationalizes the decoupling of routing policy from action execution. ZETA resolves scientific intent before invoking specialized visual tools, treating measurement as a deterministic operation grounded in explicit geometry rather than generative output. This architecture exposes the "black box" of agent decision-making, allowing routing correctness and downstream execution to be evaluated as independent failure modes.To our knowledge, we provide the first controlled study in scientific vision-agent routing that isolates explicit routing-policy specification while holding the legal action interface fixed. Evaluation on a zero-shot benchmark of 51 scientific-intent queries shows that explicit routing semantics can substantially improve routing accuracy, particularly at semantically adjacent action boundaries, although improvements vary across models. For Qwen 3.8, explicit routing-policy specification improves segmentation routing accuracy from 6.2% to 75.0% and detection routing accuracy from 60.0% to 100%. ZETA's execution traces make routing decisions and downstream artifacts separately observable, providing a basis for distinguishing intent-selection errors from visual execution failures. ZETA establishes the necessary infrastructure to isolate execution errors from interpretive ones, a critical requirement for deploying reliable scientific vision agents.
  </details>

- **[An Agentic Framework for Quality-Aware and Scenario-Adaptive Image Compression](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.04960)**  `arXiv:2611.04960`  
  _Zhenghao Chen, Lebin Zhou, Zicong Chen, Naifu Xue, Jiahao Li, Bin Li, et al._
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Despite decades of progress, image codecs remain difficult to adapt to diverse real-world compression scenarios for two main reasons. First, most image codecs are optimized for a specific objective and require substantial redevelopment when the compression goal changes. Second, they typically assume clean inputs, whereas sensor-captured images often contain degradations that alter rate-quality behavior. To address these challenges, we propose Practical Image Coding Agents (PICA), a multi-agent framework that adapts existing codecs to diverse user requirements and potentially degraded inputs. PICA consists of four collaborative agents: a Perception agent that interprets user intent and analyzes image content, an Improvement agent that jointly considers bitrate and reconstruction quality to guide pre-coding restoration, a Coding agent that refines quality-control settings from global to regional levels, and an After-coding improvement agent that addresses residual degradations and compression-induced artifacts through restoration guided solely by image quality. To enable codec-agnostic regional adaptation, we introduce Agentic ROI Coding (AROIC), which treats the codec as a black box and allows the agent to automatically schedule, execute, evaluate, and reflect ROI coding plans without architectural modifications or codec-specific retraining. We integrate these four agents with a Scenario-Guided Quality-Rate (SGQR) evaluation strategy to enable more effective scenario-adaptive compression across heterogeneous codecs. Comprehensive experiments on clean, noisy, and blurred images across standard, perceptual, and machine-vision compression scenarios demonstrate that PICA consistently enhances the compression performance of both the conventional H.266/VVC codec and the neural Cheng2020 codec, outperforming competing compression methods on the Kodak, CLIC2020, and HEVC datasets.
  </details>

- **[Mesh-Agnostic Refinement Models for Latent Space Encoding of 3D Human Body Shapes](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.03285)**  `arXiv:2611.03285`  
  _Chaima Zouaoui, Jonathan Cerqueira, Sylvain Arguillere, Martin Bauer, Nicolas Charon, Mohamed Daoudi, et al._
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Parametric human body models such as the Skinned Multi-Person Linear (SMPL) model provide compact representations of human shape and pose, but their reconstructions remain affected by both errors in estimated latent parameters and limitations in the decoder's expressive capacity. We propose a framework for refining these reconstructions by exploiting the geometric discrepancy between an initial decoded surface and a target mesh, without requiring vertex correspondences between them. The framework comprises three complementary approaches. Latent-VaRefine uses varifold distance gradients to correct the estimated latent code while preserving the original parametric representation. Vertex-VaRefine processes multiscale varifold-gradient features with a DiffusionNet backbone to predict vertex displacements in a canonical pose, yielding an approximately pose-equivariant refinement pipeline. ElaOpt directly optimizes surface deformations under elastic regularization and normal direction constraints. On AMASS, Vertex-VaRefine reduces the mean vertex-to-vertex error of OmniFit reconstructions from 1.181 to 0.342 cm, a 71.0 percent reduction, while combining Latent-VaRefine with ElaOpt reduces the asymmetric Chamfer distance of ArtEq reconstructions from 1.681 to 0.717 cm, a 57.3 percent reduction. Evaluations with SMPL-H and SMPL-X demonstrate the framework's adaptability to different body models, while additional experiments on remeshed targets and raw scans assess its robustness to changes in discretization and geometry beyond the parametric model. These results highlight the complementary strengths of latent space correction, learned vertex refinement, and elastic optimization, offering different trade-offs between preserving the model parameterization and improving geometric fidelity.
  </details>

- **[Lookahead Prediction-Guided Adaptive Visual Refocusing for Interleaved Multimodal Reasoning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.02780)**  `arXiv:2611.02780`  
  _Mengzhao Wang, Yanli Ji, Peng Ye_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Interleaved multimodal chain-of-thought reasoning improves the visual reasoning capabilities of multimodal large language models by dynamically incorporating visual evidence during reasoning. However, existing methods primarily select evidence from historical context. When the reasoning focus shifts, history-guided evidence may remain focused on prior regions and fail to cover the visual information required by the next step. We refer to this lag between visual evidence and subsequent reasoning demands as Temporal Evidence Myopia. To address this issue, we propose Lookahead Prediction-guided Adaptive Visual Refocusing (LPAVR), a training-free test-time framework. LPAVR transforms Multi-Token Prediction (MTP) from a decoding acceleration mechanism into a lookahead signal for anticipating upcoming reasoning intent. During MTP decoding, the draft head generates multiple future tokens, while the target model verifies them in parallel and retains the longest prefix consistent with its decoding trajectory. This target-verified prefix contains near-future semantics, which LPAVR uses to construct lookahead-guided visual evidence and assess whether history-guided evidence covers the indicated regions. If the coverage is sufficient, the history-guided evidence is retained; otherwise, LPAVR switches to the lookahead-guided evidence. This better aligns the visual context with upcoming reasoning and improves consistency between draft predictions and target-model decoding. Experiments on multiple multimodal reasoning benchmarks show that LPAVR improves both reasoning accuracy and the acceptance rates of MTP speculative tokens, jointly enhancing visual reasoning and speculative decoding efficiency.
  </details>

- **[PixelBench: Can LLMs Understand and Generate Images Pixel by Pixel?](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.02540)**  `arXiv:2611.02540`  
  _Haoquan Zhang, Feiyang Liu, Juanxi Tian, Wanhua Li, Haodong Duan, Weiyang Liu_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Large language models (LLMs) can generate visual assets through text-based formats such as SVG and CAD, but these symbolic representations describe images using high-level primitives rather than explicit raster values. We ask whether LLMs can instead generate pixel images directly through their existing vocabulary, without a learned image tokenizer or decoder. We introduce PixelBench, a benchmark for text-to-pixel (T2P) and image-to-pixel (I2P) generation across multiple resolutions, together with a complementary pixel-understanding evaluation. Models generate an RGB color palette followed by a grid of indices specifying the palette color of each output pixel. In T2P, the strongest models produce recognizable images directly from text. In I2P, the strongest models outperform palette-matched downsampling and specialized pixelization algorithms at low resolutions. Pixel-understanding performance correlates strongly with generation performance. A resolution-scaling study shows that pixel-generation performance often improves initially before declining at high resolutions. Finally, we introduce Pixel Reconstruction Tuning (PRT), which augments visual instruction tuning with caption-palette-grid trajectories. We post-train Molmo2-4B from its pretraining checkpoint by mixing general instruction data with our curated PRT data, improving performance across 16 visual-centric benchmarks, indicating that explicit pixel reconstruction can provide useful auxiliary supervision.
  </details>

- **[A Straight Line Is Not a Camera Pose: Auditing Short-Clip Pose Benchmarks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.00482)**  `arXiv:2611.00482`  
  _Xinyi Shi_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  The absolute trajectory error (ATE) is the standard measure of camera-motion accuracy, from SLAM to feed-forward 3D reconstruction. On the common Sintel protocol, an image-free constant-velocity line has a lower mean ATE than 10 of 11 recent models re-run with official code and than 85 of 110 published methods. On Lightspeed it beats 5 of 9 models and 10 of 11 published methods, while on TUM, ScanNet, DyCheck and ADT every model beats it. Two properties of ATE's alignment explain this. First, it maps any moving constant-velocity prediction onto the line that best fits the true path, so the line scores the path's regression residual. A residual signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) criterion tells when moving a prediction towards its constant-velocity fit lowers ATE. With the alignment's first-order refit, it accounts for the outcome of all but one of 4010 model-clip evaluations, including all 504 on three benchmarks registered before any model ran. The true path's straightness flags Sintel and Lightspeed. Second, the alignment ignores where cameras look: rotating a trajectory by 30 degrees against its orientations leaves ATE unchanged yet worsens the static-point reprojection of every model on Sintel, TUM and ScanNet, and the line reprojects worst on Sintel by geometric mean. Fitting the alignment's rotation to the predicted orientations gives pose-anchored ATE (PA-ATE), a one-function change at about ATE's cost (37 vs. 34 $\mu$s per clip, and 61 vs. 66 $\mu$s with the rotation error). It is never below ATE and, as we prove, equals the translational relative pose error over all frame pairs divided by $\sqrt{2}$ when the orientations agree. It ranks every image-free reference below every model on Sintel, follows the reprojection error where ATE does not, and largely preserves the models' order. Its rotation error also exposes Lightspeed ground-truth orientations that the images contradict.
  </details>

- **[MoRE-GS: Motion-Regime Experts for Future Gaussian Splatting](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.00375)**  `arXiv:2611.00375`  
  _Shima Salehi, Joshua Peeples_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Future dynamic novel-view synthesis requires extrapolating multiple motion regimes within the same scene. A single dynamics model may not simultaneously represent stationary regions, coordinated motion, local interactions, and articulated trajectories. We introduce Motion Regime Expert Routing for Gaussian Splatting (MoRE-GS), a causal, render-aware framework for forecasting dynamic 3D Gaussian scenes. MoRE-GS freezes a Gaussian representation reconstructed exclusively from the observed temporal prefix and forecasts its control-keypoint motion using four complementary experts: persistence, a coefficient-space Transformer, a graph convolutional network, and a structured Transformer with rigid and non-rigid motion constraints. A compact routing table assigns expert mixtures across soft motion groups and forecast-horizon bins, while a persistence gate suppresses unreliable extrapolation. Across D-NeRF and HyperNeRF scenes, MoRE-GS achieves improved performance against other methods, and these results demonstrate that renderer-calibrated composition of complementary motion predictors improves causal dynamic Gaussian forecasting across heterogeneous motion regimes.Project page:this https URL
  </details>

- **[Dynamic Merging Mutually-Distilled Multi-View Networks for RGB-Event-based Representation Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.00107)**  `arXiv:2611.00107`  
  _Futian Wang, Fan Zhang, Xiao Wang, Yuhe Ding, Shiao Wang, Jingxi Huang, et al._
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Multi-modal fusion algorithms combining conventional frame-based cameras and event cameras have recently attracted substantial research attention. Typically, existing approaches convert event streams into frames, voxels, or tensors, and then learn the required spatiotemporal information from these transformed event representations for fusion with conventional frame-camera data. Obviously, such paradigms only exploit the limited representational capacity of event data. Moreover, standard training pipelines fail to fully leverage diverse model parameters obtained throughout the learning process. In this paper, we propose a novel mutual distillation method leveraging multi-view teacher network weights to better integrate multiple event representations and achieve model-parameter level fusion. Specifically, we employ multiple encoders to extract different types of event representations and perform mutual knowledge distillation at both the feature-level and logit-level in this process. Afterwards, we perform a dynamic hierarchical model merge strategy on the model parameters from the first stage to yield a unified multi-modal RGB-Event representation model. Experimental results across multiple event-based datasets demonstrate that our proposed framework achieves significant performance improvements.
  </details>

- **[DEQ-Stereo: Deep Euilibrium Video Stereo Matching via Adaptive Convergence](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.39701)**  `arXiv:2610.39701`  
  _Kiljoon Han, Kyumin Hwang, Wonhyeok Choi, Jeonghoon Kim, Sunghoom Im_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Iterative refinement models have significantly improved stereo matching accuracy, but their rigid, fixed update schedules incur heavy computational costs and a strict trade-off between speed and accuracy. This challenge is magnified in video streams, where traditional online methods resort to reducing feature channels or relying on expensive temporal warping. To address this, we propose DEQ-Stereo, a novel video stereo matching framework based on the Deep Equilibrium (DEQ) paradigm. Instead of unrolling a fixed number of iterations, DEQ-Stereo reformulates the refinement as an implicit fixed-point problem, adaptively terminating once convergence is met. To ensure fast and stable intra-frame convergence, we introduce the Convolutional Simplified Gated Unit (ConvSGU), which eliminates unnecessary non-linearities by modeling the latent state as a gated, element-wise sum of inputs. Furthermore, to exploit cross-frame temporal coherence, we propose Temporal State Transfer (TST), a warm-start strategy that propagates the converged hidden state to the next frame without requiring explicit pose or warping priors. Extensive evaluations demonstrate that DEQ-Stereo delivers state-of-the-art performance with a superior accuracy-to-latency trade-off.
  </details>

- **[Semantic Concept Steering Breaks the Explanation Drift Loop in Continual Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.33877)**  `arXiv:2610.33877`  
  _Yehonatan Elisha, Oren Barkan, Noam Koenigstein_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Catastrophic forgetting in continual learning (CL) manifests not only as accuracy degradation but also as \emph{explanation drift}: models maintain predictive accuracy while silently shifting attention from diagnostic features to spurious correlations. This work identifies and resolves a previously overlooked structural flaw in explanation-aware CL: pixel-level saliency regularization derives supervision targets from the model's own frozen saliency maps, creating a \emph{self-referential drift loop} that actively reinforces spurious attention across tasks. We introduce \textbf{C$^3$L} (Concept-Consistent Continual Learning), which breaks this loop by anchoring regularization to class-consistent semantic concepts (e.g., ``curved beak'', ``striped pattern'') discovered offline, independent of model state, providing (i) target independence from model drift, and (ii) cross-instance semantic consistency across every instance of a class. We identify that our concept-based objective, combined with approximate LRP relevance conservation, induces a \emph{crowding-out effect}: since concept and background regions compete for the relevance of the same prediction, enforcing high relevance within concept regions implicitly suppresses spurious background correlations without explicit penalization. \method does not require human-annotated concept sets, as it employs a fully automated concept discovery and spatial grounding. Extensive evaluation across five benchmarks and over 20 baselines demonstrates state-of-the-art performance in accuracy, forgetting, explanation quality, spurious correlation mitigation, and out-of-distribution robustness.
  </details>

- **[Whispers from the Neighbors: Rethinking Caption Consensus as Inference-Time Evidence for Vision-Language Retrieval](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.33798)**  `arXiv:2610.33798`  
  _Khang Nhat Hoang Vo, Belal Shoer, Abhirama Subramanyam Penamakuri_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  An image is rarely described only once. Retrieval benchmarks and many collections attach several captions to each picture, yet dual encoders still judge every image-caption pair in isolation. We ask what these neighboring captions contribute when a frozen encoder consults them at inference time. Fusing image similarity with similarity to an image's own captions improves text-to-image R@1 by 3.4 to 16.8 points across nine frozen encoders when the captions come from the same annotators as the queries. The gain falls to 1.9 to 7.2 points when an off-the-shelf captioner writes them, and to at most one point when they come from a different annotation source; a paraphrase-trained text encoder strengthens the text side further. A natural refinement, scoring the part of the image that the captions leave unexplained, appears to add much more under a leave-one-out evaluation. We show that this advantage arises because the correct candidate's supports are built differently from those of the negative candidates, with set size and query removal each contributing about half, and that under a fixed support index the residual reduces to a reweighting of what the captions already provide. On compositional benchmarks, the captions help by matching candidates to human descriptions of the image, without improving image-text grounding. The code is available at:this https URL
  </details>

- **[ReCoG: Relational Concept Graph for Training-Free Personalization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.31282)**  `arXiv:2610.31282`  
  _Changseon Yu, Hyeokjun Kweon_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Training-free personalization adapts a frozen vision-language model (VLM) to recognize user-defined concepts from only a few exemplars by retrieving concept entries at inference time. While recent retriever-based methods enrich each concept with descriptive evidence, they largely treat concepts in isolation, so the retrieved information can be plausible yet non-discriminative, especially when the personalized concept set contains highly confusable, fine-grained categories. We argue that personalization is inherently relational: correct recognition depends on the specific distinctions between a concept and its nearest alternatives. To this end, we propose ReCoG, a Relational Concept Graph for retrieval-augmented personalization. ReCoG represents concepts as nodes and augments them with directed edges that explicitly capture discriminative cues between concept pairs, elicited by a frozen VLM during database construction. At inference, ReCoG retrieves a shortlist and resolves ambiguity via explicit pairwise comparisons conditioned on the corresponding relational edges, selecting the concept that consistently wins against competing candidates. We also introduce FINGER benchmark to test personalized recognition on confusable concept sets. Across FINGER, ReCoG substantially outperforms prior methods, with the largest gains in the most confusable regimes. ReCoG also achieves consistently best performance on established personalization benchmarks including captioning and VQA, confirming that relational evidence is broadly beneficial beyond fine-grained settings. Project Page:this https URL
  </details>

- **[TriTD: Tri-Partite Trajectory-Distribution Distillation for Real-Time Autoregressive Video Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.26165)**  `arXiv:2610.26165`  
  _Jia Li, Xurui Peng, Haowei Zhu, Tianyu Zhao, Jiexi Wang, Youwei Zheng, et al._
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Autoregressive (AR) video diffusion has emerged as a leading paradigm for efficient video generation, yet its practical deployment remains bottlenecked by the trade-off between generation quality and inference efficiency. We attribute this bottleneck to three error sources in AR rollouts: the base model error, the train-inference distribution mismatch, and the upstream error propagation. Building on this decomposition, we derive closed-form upper bounds on the per-step and cumulative errors, providing a principled basis for jointly optimizing generation quality and inference efficiency. Guided by this analysis, we propose TriTD, a Tri-Partite Trajectory-Distribution co-optimized distillation framework with three complementary modules. First, for ODE initialization, we adopt a Next-Node Trajectory Distillation (NTD) objective, which shortens the supervision horizon and admits a lower regression-error floor. Second, we introduce Chunk-Graded Noising (CGN), a monotonically non-decreasing per-chunk noising schedule that helps narrow the expected train-inference noise mismatch and removes redundant KV-cache updates, yielding substantial speedups at no quality cost. Third, we propose Orthogonal-Parallel DMD (OP-DMD), a distribution-matching loss that retains the original DMD supervision while introducing an additional regression constraint in the orthogonal subspace to suppress off-axis drift, improving both training stability and final generation quality. Extensive experiments show that TriTD consistently surpasses existing baselines in visual quality while reaching a real-time throughput of 26.8 FPS on a single H100 GPU, delivering a balanced quality-efficiency solution for interactive streaming video generation.
  </details>

- **[I2V-DETACH: Source Grounding Detachment for Unauthorized Image-to-Video Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.23287)**  `arXiv:2610.23287`  
  _Chanhui Lee, Yeonghwan Song, Yewon Kang, Jeany Son_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Recent diffusion models have advanced image-conditioned video generation, but their accessibility raises risks of unauthorized manipulation. Image immunization has emerged as a promising defense for Image-to-Video (I2V) protection, yet existing methods often rely on degrading visual quality or temporal coherence. In this work, we revisit I2V immunization as reducing source-content preservation, shifting the focus from output degradation to weakening source-conditioned content propagation. To this end, we propose I2V-DETACH, an image immunization method that prevents unauthorized I2V generation through source grounding detachment. I2V models preserve source content by propagating source-image cues into video latents during denoising. Accordingly, I2V-DETACH disrupts this process in two complementary ways: it suppresses source-video grounding to reduce source cue propagation, and strengthens intra-video interactions to shift denoising toward video-side dynamics with reduced reliance on the source image. To obtain informative optimization signals, we initialize auxiliary video latents with source-oriented states that remain within the source-conditioned generation regime while deviating from source-preserving trajectories. Extensive experiments across diverse diffusion architectures show that I2V-DETACH substantially reduces source-content preservation, improves over prior immunization methods, and exhibits strong black-box transferability.
  </details>

- **[FlowSim: Rendering-Free Closed-Loop Simulation for Evaluating End-to-End Driving Systems](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.18030)**  `arXiv:2610.18030`  
  _Hanfeng Wu, Alvaro Marcos-Ramiro, Michael Schmidt, Christoph Stiller_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Closed-loop evaluation of end-to-end (E2E) driving systems typically relies on generating sensor observations and re-processing them through the perception encoder, introducing substantial computational cost and a sim2real gap between simulated and real sensor observations. In this paper, we ask a more fundamental question: is image-space simulation necessary for closed-loop evaluation of E2E driving systems? We propose FlowSim, a rendering-free simulation paradigm that predicts the internal latent representation directly from a previous latent and target-frame symbolic scene conditions. The predicted latent is then processed by the original frozen downstream modules, eliminating image rendering and perception re-encoding. Explicit cross-frame agent association improves latent transition prediction and rollout stability, while variable-horizon simulation enables long-horizon prediction from a common real anchor without accumulating intermediate rollout errors. Experiments on nuScenes and NavSim demonstrate that FlowSim preserves downstream behavior competitively with, and often exceeds image-space simulation in source-to-reference agreement across variable simulation horizons and both dense and sparse latent representations. By predicting the latent directly, both instantiations of FlowSim simulate each step in 0.04--0.06s, substantially faster than the image-space simulation methods they are compared against. These results establish FlowSim as an efficient and practical alternative to conventional image-space simulation methods. Our project page isthis https URL.
  </details>

- **[Sparse All-Layer Connector for Domain Generalised Semantic Segmentation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.15660)**  `arXiv:2610.15660`  
  _Ruoyu Guo, Xin Kun Lin, Maurice Pagnucco, Yang Song_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Domain generalised semantic segmentation (DGSS) has recently benefited from combining multiple foundation models, such as vision-language and vision foundation models, to leverage their diverse representations for generalisation. Existing multi-model approaches share a common design choice: cross-model fusion is restricted to depth-aligned layers, implicitly assuming that mutually beneficial information resides at the same depth across models. However, foundation models pretrained under different objectives may develop distinct representation hierarchies, making the optimality of depth-aligned fusion questionable. Moreover, we observe that the foundation models exhibit different depth-wise domain sensitivity. Motivated by these observations, we propose a Sparse All-Layer Connector (SALC) that enables each layer to access information from preceding layers of another model. As the number of accessible layers grows with depth, dense aggregation may hurt generalisation. SALC therefore learns to adaptively select a sparse subset of informative layers. We further introduce a candidate dropout regularisation that strengthens sparsity and encourages SALC to explore diverse layers, leading to more robust selection. Across four foundation model combinations and three DGSS evaluation settings, the proposed design demonstrates stronger generalisation than conventional depth-aligned fusion. The code is available atthis https URL.
  </details>

- **[ELMA: Benchmarking Anaphoric Compositions for Long-Term Text-to-Motion Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.13549)**  `arXiv:2610.13549`  
  _Shun Kato, Dixin Yang, Kotaro Amaya, Yuiga Wada, Kazumi Fukuda, Takashi Shibuya, et al._
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Text-guided long-term human motion generation is essential for applications such as continuously operating digital avatars. Despite recent progress on short clips, existing models struggle with multi-segment instructions that involve anaphora, where constraints established in earlier segments must be preserved over time. In this paper, we introduce a novel task of long-term motion generation from such anaphoric compositions. To address this gap, we present ELMA, an episodic long-term motion dataset with dense segment-level annotations that preserve cross-segment dependencies. Built via a fully automated collection and filtering pipeline, ELMA extracts high-quality, continuous 30-second clips from in-the-wild videos, capturing the episodic narratives necessary for long-range state modeling. Using ELMA, we benchmark representative long-term motion generation models under independent and anaphoric instruction settings, and study whether contextual fine-tuning improves long-range state modeling. Our extensive experiments provide insights into the capabilities and limitations of existing models in handling context-dependent instructions. These findings highlight the challenge of modeling cross-segment dependencies and offer valuable directions for developing more coherent and semantically consistent long-term motion generation models.
  </details>

- **[When Predicting Nothing Beats SAM 3: Revisiting Evaluation in Video Object Segmentation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02946)**  `arXiv:2610.02946`  
  _Jihwan Hong, Woohyeon Park, Jaeik Kim, Jaeyoung Do_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Video Object Segmentation (VOS) in complex and long videos is increasingly important for real-world applications, where target objects often appear only intermittently within long temporal horizons. However, existing benchmarks largely focus on temporally salient objects that remain visible for most of the video. To address this gap, we introduce FaVOS (A Benchmark for Video Object Segmentation with Fractional Temporal Visibility), a benchmark designed to evaluate VOS methods under low temporal visibility. We show that, in this regime, the standard J&F metric can collapse VOS evaluation into absence classification, because empty predictions receive high rewards on target-absent frames. Consequently, even a trivial empty-mask predictor can outperform strong models such as SAM 3, revealing a fundamental mismatch between current metrics and practical VOS performance. To mitigate this issue, we propose Volumetric J&F, which evaluates mask sequences as spatio-temporal volumes and reduces the dominance of target-absence rewards while preserving sensitivity to segmentation quality and temporal structure. Project page:this https URL.
  </details>

- **[PhyProbe: Rethinking Physical Consistency Evaluation in Generated Videos](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.38377)**  `arXiv:2609.38377`  
  _Max Ku, Jiaojiao Fan, Zekun Hao, Francesco Ferroni, Heng Wang, Wenhu Chen, et al._
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Evaluating the physical consistency of generated videos remains a fundamental challenge. Existing approaches rely on off-the-shelf vision-language models, which can often be myopic to physical dynamics, or fine-tuned evaluators trained on human annotations, which overfit to dataset-specific cues and fail to generalize. A key challenge is that existing supervision sources provide either relative ordering or absolute scores, but not both reliably and consistently across varied settings. To this end, we introduce PhyProbe, an evaluator that extracts features from a frozen pretrained spatio-temporal encoder and maps them to a scalar physical consistency violation score via a lightweight scoring head. PhyProbe is trained through a unified objective combining pairwise ranking, regression on noisy scalar annotations, and anchor-based calibration over a curated set of heterogeneous supervision sources. Experiments show that PhyProbe outperforms prior methods on most pairwise benchmarks spanning real-generated and generated-generated pairs under varying correspondence, with the largest gains in no-correspondence and generated-generated settings where existing fine-tuned evaluators degrade sharply. PhyProbe achieves strong correlation with human judgments, with close agreement between rank-based and linear metrics, indicating that scores are both well ordered and anchored to a stable [0, 1] scale. Further, despite being trained on supervision indicative of physical consistency, without explicit general-preference labels, PhyProbe also performs competitively on human preference benchmarks: consistent with the observation that physics violations are entangled with broader quality degradations.
  </details>

- **[Panoptic Scene Program Diffusion Transformer](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.31780)**  `arXiv:2609.31780`  
  _Chika Maduabuchi_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Modern text-to-image models produce high-fidelity images but still struggle with compositional prompts that require instance identity, attribute ownership, counting, spatial ordering, and role-sensitive relations. We introduce Panoptic Scene Program Diffusion Transformer (PSP-DiT), a diffusion-transformer architecture that treats a panoptic scene program as a first-class latent variable rather than an external control signal or post-hoc parse. PSP-DiT jointly denoises image latents and scene-program latents through coupled transformer streams, while panoptic grounding and cycle-consistency objectives tie object instances, attributes, relations, and counts to visual support in the generated image. Under matched training and inference settings, PSP-DiT improves over a strong flat-text baseline across GenEval 2, SANEval-Simple, PSG-Score, and DetailMaster, with the largest gains on counting, attribute binding, role-sensitive relations, and long structured prompts. The method preserves image quality, adds modest inference overhead, and remains robust to imperfect scene programs.
  </details>

- **[VideoGen-Agent: Reinforcing Video Generation Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.24997)**  `arXiv:2609.24997`  
  _Binxu Li, Haoyi Duan, Yuhui Zhang, Yaohui Zhang, Zihao Lin, Kaituo Feng, et al._
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Recent advances in video generative models have enabled high-fidelity, temporally coherent video generation. However, these models often struggle to satisfy prompts requiring specialized knowledge, specific identities, physical consistency, or ordered events. In this paper, we present VideoGen-Agent, a multimodal agent trained through multitask agentic reinforcement learning to use external tools for video generation. The agent coordinates augmentation, generation, and verification tools through multi-turn interactions, using the prompt and intermediate observations to guide its decisions. We train a shared policy on a category-balanced dataset spanning six tasks. Supervised fine-tuning on teacher-generated trajectories establishes tool-use behavior, which is then refined through reinforcement learning. A category-aware hybrid reward evaluates tool-call validity, task-appropriate tool use, and generated video quality. We further introduce VABench, a held-out benchmark of 600 prompts covering procedural knowledge, single- and multi-entity identity preservation, physical consistency, scene composition, and multi-shot temporal structure. On VABench, VideoGen-Agent improves over its base text-to-video generator by 19.1 points, from 56.5 to 75.6. Upgrading the generation tools further raises the score to 86.1 without additional agent training. Human raters prefer the upgraded configuration over the strongest standalone baseline in 84.3% of comparisons. These results support learning tool use across video-generation tasks and show that the trained agent can benefit from subsequent advances in generation tools. Project page:this https URL
  </details>

- **[Exemplar: Few-Shot Biomedical Segmentation That Fits in Seconds](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.03080)**  `arXiv:2609.03080`  
  _Michal Průšek, Adam Novozámský, Filip Šroubek_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Segmenting a new microscopy dataset usually means training a deep network on its annotations, and training again for every added image. Exemplar solves a segmentation readout in closed form and updates it exactly with each new mask in seconds, as accurately as networks trained for minutes. The updated readout is identical to a fit from all masks at once. Its linear readout combines frozen DINOv3 features, read at a magnification chosen from the masks, with classical filter responses at native resolution. Its regularisation and its pixel weighting are chosen exactly by leaving out one annotated image at a time, so none is set aside for validation. On ten biomedical datasets from cells to vessels and filaments, Exemplar is more accurate than every few-shot method that only applies a pretrained model, and on average than nnU-Net trained on the same masks. A fine-tuned Cellpose-SAM, the strongest baseline, is as accurate on average, but each of its fits takes a median of 25 minutes against 8.5 seconds, and each new mask means fine-tuning it again.
  </details>

- **[Beyond Landmark Extraction: A Framework for Robust Geometric Feature Evaluation in Structured Image Classification](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.00634)**  `arXiv:2609.00634`  
  _Saravana Mauree, Sakshi Arya_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Much of the literature on structured image recognition has disproportionately focused on the comparison of classification algorithms. Rather than investigating which classifier performs best, this paper instead asks: what should a classifier know before it ever makes a prediction? In structured vision problems such as gesture recognition, facial expression categorization, and medical image analysis, discriminative information lies less in individual pixels and more in spatial relationships between semantic parts. Raw pixel spaces are high-dimensional, sensitive to nuisance variation, and often obfuscate the geometric structures that make visual tasks interpretable. Landmark extraction provides one form of dimension reduction, but it does not by itself determine the information preserved. This paper studies the post-landmark feature map as the central object of analysis and proposes a systematic framework for constructing and interpreting landmark-derived representations as an, informed, feature-based "dimension reduction" step. Using static hand gesture recognition as a case study, we evaluate coordinate, distance, angle, and hybrid representations through perturbation and ablation experiments. The results show that visually variable data exposes substantial gaps between raw coordinate features and their geometrically invariant counterparts, while hybrid representations achieve the strongest overall performance by combining complementary geometric components. These findings frame feature construction as a fundamental modeling decision and ultimately suggests that the question of what representation should a classifier learn from is one worth asking. The code used for feature construction and evaluation is available atthis https URL
  </details>

- **[GenScale: A Benchmark for Relative Object Scale in Image Generation and Editing](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.00525)**  `arXiv:2609.00525`  
  _Lingxiao Li, Max Whitton, Ledell Wu, Boqing Gong_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Modern image generation and editing systems can produce photorealistic, prompt-aligned images, but still often render familiar objects at implausible relative sizes. To measure this failure mode, we introduce GenScale, a benchmark and evaluation protocol for real-world relative object scale in image generation and editing. GenScale contains 900 image-level entries and 1,643 pairwise anchor-target scale relations across common-object generation, human-product generation with metric dimensions, and scale correction from failed generations. We further design a human-calibrated ordinal judge for scalable pairwise scale evaluation. Last but not least, we introduce Rescale, a model-agnostic post-processing agent for localized scale correction without modifying the source generator. Experiments reveal that state-of-the-art image generators and editors do not reliably render plausible relative scale, while Rescale consistently improves scale plausibility across generated and edited images. Together, GenScale establishes relative object scale as a distinct, measurable, and actionable capability for image generation systems.
  </details>

- **[MEDR: Query-Independent Frame Selection via Multi-Signal Event Modeling and Dynamic Rescoring](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.15058)**  `arXiv:2608.15058`  
  _Xinlei Pu, Weijie Shi, Wen Yang, Yi Cao, Yao Zhao, Hao Chen, et al._
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Frame selection is a fundamental component of multimodal large language models, enabling long videos to be processed under limited visual-token and computational budgets. Uniform sampling preserves temporal coverage but may miss informative content that appears only briefly. To alleviate this limitation, query-dependent methods can retrieve question-relevant frames. However, because the selected frames depend on the current question, the same visual input cannot be directly shared across different questions, and frame selection must be repeated in multi-turn video dialogue. This motivates us to seek a query-independent frame selection method that preserves the reusability of a fixed visual input while improving the coverage of informative events beyond uniform sampling. We propose Multi-Signal Event Modeling and Dynamic Rescoring (MEDR), a training-free and query-independent frame selection method. Multi-Signal Event Modeling organizes complementary visual, motion, and text signals into signal-specific temporal events. Dynamic Rescoring then iteratively reevaluates each candidate relative to the current selected set, updating its score according to frame-level signal strength, additional event coverage, and balanced temporal coverage. The resulting fixed frame set is constructed without observing the query and can be reused across different questions. Experiments on Video-MME and LongVideoBench demonstrate that MEDR achieves competitive performance across two video MLLMs. Under the 64-frame budget, MEDR improves Video-MME accuracy over the strongest evaluated query-independent baseline by 1.33-1.78 percentage points. We further evaluate the reuse of a fixed frame set in multi-question video dialogue.
  </details>

- **[What to Preserve, Where to Adapt: A Depth-Wise Analysis of Forgetting in Continual Gynecological Image Segmentation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.13660)**  `arXiv:2608.13660`  
  _Amal Saqib, Tausifa Jan Saleem, Numan Saeed, Mohammad Yaqub_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  The clinical management of gynecological diseases often relies on medical imaging for diagnosis, treatment planning, and follow-up. Segmentation in this setting is challenging because successive tasks may differ in imaging modality, target anatomy, pathology, and annotation structure. Continual learning allows models to adapt to new tasks without simultaneous access to previous datasets. However, when successive tasks differ substantially, learning a new task can degrade performance on earlier ones, a problem known as catastrophic forgetting. Understanding where adaptation disrupts previous knowledge can help guide the design of more targeted continual-learning strategies. We investigate how forgetting changes as different parts of an encoder--decoder network are allowed to adapt. We progressively expand the trainable region of a 3D nnU-Net backbone from the bottleneck toward input- and output-proximal blocks. Under a shared learning rate, adaptation near the bottleneck largely preserves previous-task performance but provides limited current-task learning, whereas broader adaptation improves current-task performance but sharply increases forgetting. This trade-off persists even when the average change in trainable backbone parameters is approximately comparable. Assigning different learning rates to different blocks substantially reduces forgetting when part of the backbone is trainable, although this changes both the size and location of the updates. Forgetting still increases as more blocks are trained and remains severe when the full backbone is updated. These results show that forgetting depends not only on how much the model changes, but also on which parts of the model are allowed to change.
  </details>

- **[Hold-Out Self-Validation Cannot Certify the Accuracy of Photogrammetric Reconstructions](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.24852)**  `arXiv:2607.24852`  
  _Behnam Asadi_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Photogrammetric reconstructions used for inspection are often delivered without an independent accuracy check. Hold-out self-validation is a possible substitute. Images are withheld, their orientations are re-estimated from the rest of the block, and agreement is taken as evidence of quality. We test it on ten GNSS-referenced aerial captures from eight sites, on ETH3D and EuRoC, and on 30 IMC 2025 scenes. The standard form re-localises each withheld image only against points seen by at least two retained images. Its score saturates. It stayed at 1.00 in all 40 thinned reconstructions while camera-position error varied by a factor of up to 5.9 within one capture. It also scored 1.00 on a corrupted model with only one of 226 cameras within 5 m. Reprojection error ranked some of the worst models best. A few lost cameras can raise the least-squares RMSE to the size of the block, so we also evaluate with a robust alignment. Taking the correspondences from the verified matches lowered the score below 0.95 in 14 of 18 corrupted runs, against 4 for the standard form and 10 when its failed resections count as errors, with all seven nominal runs at 1.00. Mapping the block again without the withheld images also responds, but mapping the same corrupted data twice without withholding gave a similar disagreement, so the signal is mainly that a corrupted reconstruction is not reproducible. Neither test can see an error that every reconstruction repeats, and neither can replace check points.
  </details>

- **[Accuracy potential of visual localization exploiting high-end street-level imagery](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.24409)**  `arXiv:2607.24409`  
  _Jonas Meyer, Stephan Nebiker, Pascal Theiler, Norbert Haala_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Many applications, such as surveying, autonomous navigation, robotics and augmented reality, require accurate pose information with respect to a reference frame. Visual localization can complement GNSS positioning, whose availability and accuracy are often limited. However, the accuracy potential of visual localization has not yet been systematically investigated against survey-grade requirements, and no publicly available large-scale outdoor dataset provides ground-truth poses accurate enough for such an investigation. We address both gaps. First, we present the FHNW Muttenz dataset. It covers a contiguous 10 km street network, mapped in two mobile mapping campaigns about 1.5 years apart, and comprises high-resolution reference imagery as well as query sequences from four cameras in five scenes. The two campaigns are co-registered to each other with an accuracy of 5 mm. Co-registration of the query images to the reference imagery yields ground-truth poses accurate to 6-9 mm in position and well below 0.1° in orientation. All images are georeferenced with an accuracy of about 2.5 cm. Second, we use this dataset to systematically evaluate sparse feature-based visual localization with a modular pipeline built from established components, using the high-resolution reference imagery directly as the scene representation. For daytime imagery and pre-calibrated cameras, the median pose errors with respect to the reference imagery are 1-5 cm in translation and 0.03-0.1° in rotation. Given an accurately georeferenced scene representation, visual localization not only approaches the accuracy of survey-grade GNSS positioning but also provides full orientation information. The dataset is publicly available atthis https URL
  </details>

- **[Latent Riemannian Flow Matching for Geometry-Grounded 3D Foundation Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.19120)**  `arXiv:2607.19120`  
  _Lisa Weijler, Irene Ballester, Guofeng Mei, Tolga Birdal, Pedro Hermosilla_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Geometric foundation models such as the Visual Geometry Grounded Transformer (VGGT) provide strong 3D priors from unposed images, but operate deterministically and cannot generate plausible geometry beyond what the observations directly support. We bridge geometric foundation models and generative 3D modeling by performing flow matching directly in their latent space, leveraging learned 3D priors without committing to explicit representations such as Gaussians, meshes, or video-VAE latents. This requires respecting the latent geometry: LayerNorm places the decoder inputs on a product of zero-mean hyperspheres, and treating this space as unconstrained Euclidean substantially degrades flow matching. We therefore formulate Riemannian flow matching on this product manifold, conditioned on unposed context views and a target camera pose, keeping generated tokens within the geometry expected by the frozen decoder. Our main experiments use VGGT, while additional experiments with Depth Anything 3 show that the same formulation transfers to a different independently pretrained 3D backbone without modification. On RealEstate10K, ScanNet++, and ETH3D, our method achieves strong results against recent scene-generation baselines in both novel-view appearance and aggregated 3D geometry, establishing latent-space flow matching on geometric foundation models as a viable paradigm for 3D generation.
  </details>

- **[LPM: Industrial-Scale Generative Video Restoration](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.13460)**  `arXiv:2607.13460`  
  _Bichuan Zhu, Fulin Li, Jiachao Gong, Jinhua Hao, Kai Zhao, Kun Yuan, et al._
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  We present the Large Processing Model (LPM), a diffusion-based generative framework for photorealistic video restoration under complex, in-the-wild degradations. To our knowledge, LPM is the first generative video restoration model deployed at industrial scale. LPM addresses the diverse degradations in user-generated content (UGC) through a unified system encompassing large-scale data engineering, foundation-model training, and efficient inference. Its enhanced architecture, progressive training strategy, and temporal-pyramid inference mechanism jointly enable high-fidelity, temporally consistent restoration of arbitrarily long videos across the broad content distribution encountered on UGC platforms. LPM has been deployed in production at Kuaishou, where videos processed by the model account for approximately 45% of total viewing time, delivering consistent improvements across key quality-of-experience metrics. Beyond perceptual enhancement, LPM delivers substantial system-level benefits: at comparable perceptual quality, it reduces bitrate by 20% relative to Kuaishou's in-house codec, yielding annual bandwidth cost savings on the order of hundreds of millions. Its low serving cost also enables integration into products such as Kling, demonstrating that generative restoration can be practical, scalable, and cost-effective for large-scale video processing.
  </details>

- **[Steering Training Trajectories in Diffusion Representation Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.05319)**  `arXiv:2607.05319`  
  _Rajat Rasal, Avinash Kori, Tian Xia, Ben Glocker_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Across training runs of a diffusion autoencoder, we observe similar image reconstruction quality, but substantially different levels of disentanglement in the learned representations. In this work, we study how training dynamics contribute to this behaviour. By analysing training trajectories in a controlled setting - curves of reconstruction quality against disentanglement during training - we identify two recurring trajectory patterns, which we call learning regimes. These regimes differ in how reconstruction and disentanglement evolve, despite similar reconstruction at the end of training. In the reconstruction regime, models improve image fidelity before disentanglement, while in the disentanglement regime, models improve both reconstruction and disentanglement more gradually. We hypothesise that modulating shortcut pathways in the diffusion U-Net and controlling early noise-level exposure can shape trajectories. To that end, we introduce SteeringDRL, combining gated residual U-Nets with a noise curriculum to steer models towards better disentanglement. Across attribute disentanglement benchmarks, SteeringDRL has competitive disentanglement, with reduced seed sensitivity in many settings. Our method extends to spatial disentanglement with object-centric learning, improving unsupervised segmentation on synthetic and real-world datasets.
  </details>

- **[Emergence of a Shared Canonical Object Frame from In-the-Wild Videos](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.30058)**  `arXiv:2606.30058`  
  _Tom Fischer, Martin Sundermeyer, Adam Kortylewski, Eddy Ilg_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Comparing object orientations and positions across different instances requires their poses to be expressed in a shared canonical frame. Establishing such frames has traditionally required manual annotation, creating a scaling bottleneck that limits category and instance diversity. We show that a shared canonical frame can instead emerge from self-supervised training on object-centric videos of rigid objects captured in the wild, using only noisy camera poses from Structure-from-Motion. Our key idea is to route all training sequences through a shared geometric bottleneck: a coarse canonical mesh that carries no category-specific detail. By learning dense correspondences from image pixels to this mesh, and estimating per-sequence alignments from noisy SfM geometry, a common canonical frame emerges from multi-view consistency and the semantic priors of the feature extractor, without any canonical pose labels or category conditioning. Trained in a self-supervised manner on ${\sim}160{,}000$ in-the-wild object videos, our method achieves competitive accuracy on category-level pose estimation benchmarks compared to methods that rely on canonical pose supervision. The code and checkpoint are available on \href{this https URL}{this http URL}.
  </details>

- **[TACO: Towards Task-Consistent Open-Vocabulary Adaptation in Video Recognition](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.25478)**  `arXiv:2606.25478`  
  _Minghao Zhu, Xiao Lin, Mengxian Hu, Xun Zhou, Liuyi Wang, Xiaoyan Qi, et al._
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Adapting CLIP for open-vocabulary video recognition necessitates a delicate balance between newly acquired video knowledge and the pretrained generalization. While existing studies pursue this generalization-specialization trade-off with additional regularizations or constraints, we argue that they overlook the deviation of representations beyond the fine-tuning data distribution, resulting in suboptimal adaptation effects. We believe such deviation is inherited from the inconsistency between the fine-tuning and evaluation objectives, where model optimization is restricted to the known training distribution but evaluated on unseen ones. In this paper, we introduce \emph{TACO}, a simple yet effective framework to mitigate the potential negative effects induced by this inconsistency. Our key insight is that adaptation should preserve OOD-relevant alignment beyond the training distribution. To this end, we propose \emph{Relative Structure Distillation}, which regularizes the relative geometry of the representation space and suppresses harmful alignment shift during training. We further decouple the representation space from the optimization space with a lightweight specialization projection, allowing task-specific adaptation without directly overspecializing the representations used at test time. \emph{TACO} establishes state-of-the-art performance on diverse benchmarks under cross-dataset and base-to-novel settings. Code will be released atthis https URL.
  </details>

- **[Text-Driven Fusion for Infrared and Visible Images: Achieving Image Scene Adaptation on Hyperbolic Space](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.15104)**  `arXiv:2606.15104`  
  _Huan Kang, Hui Li, Tianyang Xu, Tao Zhou, Xiao-Jun Wu, Josef Kittler_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Infrared and visible image fusion aims to integrate complementary modalities, while existing Euclidean methods impose rigid distance metrics that distort multi-modal interactions and parent-to-child semantic hierarchies. To overcome these limitations, we introduce a text-driven fusion framework empowered by hyperbolic manifold learning. During training, BLIP-extracted text prompts serve as topological anchors within the hyperbolic space, guiding vision-attribute alignment through hyperbolic embeddings that naturally accommodate varying semantic granularities. By exploiting the exponential volume growth dictated by the Poincaré ball's negative curvature, this approach seamlessly embeds hierarchical trees to encode coarse-to-fine semantics without metric saturation, while the vast peripheral space prevents texture distortion during cross-modal fusion. At inference, the fusion process autonomously adapts to input content using the learned text-attribute priors, completely eliminating the need for textual input. Experimental results show our method outperforms state-of-the-art approaches on benchmark datasets, with code available atthis https URL.
  </details>

- **[EGOSTREAM: A Diagnostic Benchmark for Streaming Episodic Memory in Egocentric Vision](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.31557)**  `arXiv:2605.31557`  
  _Rosario Forte, Giuseppe Lando, Antonino Furnari_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Continuous episodic memory is a core capability for autonomous agents operating in dynamic, real-world environments, yet current streaming video benchmarks provide limited tools for diagnosing what models remember and for how long. We introduce EGOSTREAM, a diagnostic benchmark for streaming episodic memory evaluation in egocentric vision. EGOSTREAM organizes 2,250 curated questions along seven cognitive dimensions: detail, spatial, temporal, event, social, causal, and prospective memory. We introduce the Answer Validity Window (AVW), which specifies the temporal span an answer remains valid as the observed scene evolves. This allows us to expand the questions into 8,528 recall-conditioned evaluations, enabling controlled testing from instant to ultra-long-term recall while separating genuine model forgetting from natural world-state changes. We rigorously establish baseline performance through a unified streaming MLLM framework that compares several state-of-the-art memory-management mechanisms, covering sliding windows, attention sinks, KV-cache pruning, merging, adaptive head budgets, and offloading. Experiments on a unified Qwen3-VL backbone, with consistent trends on Molmo2-8B and InternVL3.5-8B, reveal that comparable aggregate accuracies mask starkly different memory profiles. For instance, token pruning preserves fine-grained details and temporal structure significantly better than token merging, adaptive head budgets yield the highest aggregate semantic accuracy, while quantized offloading rescues ultra-long-term recall. Ultimately, all in-cache memory policies operate well below real-time (>1s per frame), and top performing in-cache methods ceil at about 45% accuracy under a 9,804-token budget, exposing critical gaps in current architectures. EGOSTREAM provides the diagnostic testbed needed to close these gaps. Project website:this https URL
  </details>

- **[No Safe Dose: How Training Data Drives Unsafe Image Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.28137)**  `arXiv:2605.28137`  
  _Felix Friedrich, Lukas Helff, Niharika Hegde, Patrick Schramowski, Kristian Kersting_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Text-to-image models are trained on web-scale data that inevitably contains unsafe images, yet whether this contamination directly drives unsafe generation has not been tested under controlled conditions. We train the same text-to-image model on corpora that differ only in their fraction of unsafe images (0% to 9.6%) and in size (100K to 8M), and evaluate 10,000 generations per model with four independent safety classifiers. Output unsafety rises monotonically and saturates, from 16.6% at 0% to 26.4% at 9.6% contamination, and the effect appears only under adversarial prompts. At a fixed training budget, the level is set by the proportion of unsafe images rather than their absolute count or cumulative exposure, so filtering a fixed fraction is equally effective at 1M and 8M images, at no measurable cost in FID, CLIPScore, or ImageReward. Filtering alone, however, does not eliminate unsafe generation: a floor persists when every image flagged by any of four judges is removed (13.6%) and rises when training on real instead of synthetic images (23.1%). A safety-aligned text encoder lowers the floor to 9.6%, but it is not carried by a removable encoder direction, which implicates the generative backbone. Finally, fine-tuning on entirely safe data erodes the benefit of curation (+8.7pp). Data curation and encoder choice are complementary and effective, but neither makes a model safe on its own.
  </details>

- **[SliceWorld: A Predictive and Controllable World-State Model for CT Report Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.24371)**  `arXiv:2605.24371`  
  _Yuanhe Tian, Yan Song_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  CT report generation (CTRG) requires models to summarize three-dimensional anatomical context and pathological findings from hundreds of axial slices. Existing methods typically learn a direct image-to-text mapping, providing limited mechanisms for modeling how CT evidence evolves across slices or how reports respond to controlled changes in latent lesion-related factors. We propose SliceWorld, a CT-specific world-state framework that treats an axial CT scan as an ordered sequence along the z-axis. SliceWorld encodes prefix CT evidence into factor-aware latent states containing anatomy, lesion, and uncertainty components, and projects these states into world tokens used for multi-step future-slice feature prediction, lesion-factor intervention, and LLM-based report generation. The model is first pretrained on CT slice sequences with predictive, factor-aware, and counterfactual objectives, and is then fine-tuned on paired CT-report data. Experiments on M3D-Cap and CT-RATE show that SliceWorld improves natural language generation metrics and clinically oriented automatic evaluation. Further analyses demonstrate multi-horizon future-slice prediction, measurable factor alignment, reduced-slice robustness, and selective lesion-sensitive report modulation. Code is available atthis https URL.
  </details>

- **[Oracle Supervision Transfers for Hyperparameter Prediction in Model-Based Image Denoising](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.20479)**  `arXiv:2605.20479`  
  _Jianmin Liao, Lixin Shen, Yuesheng Xu_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Hyperparameter prediction is a critical practical bottleneck for model-based image denoisers, ranging from classical TV/TGV variational solvers to modern diffusion-based models such as DiffPIR. While existing learned predictors can achieve near-oracle performance, this approach scales poorly: each new configuration conventionally requires its own oracle-labeled training set, and each label requires a hierarchical grid search evaluated against clean ground truth. We therefore ask whether oracle supervision collected on source configurations can transfer to target configurations with few or no target oracle labels. We propose HyperDn, a single configuration-conditioned predictor that pools oracle supervision across source configurations and predicts heterogeneous hyperparameters for new denoiser--noise configurations. In a cross-paradigm experiment, HyperDn transfers from relatively cheap TV/TGV variational sources to more expensive diffusion-based DiffPIR. With only $2$ target oracle labels, it reaches $30.23$\,dB, within $0.90$\,dB of the oracle, and outperforms the $64$-label per-configuration predictor trained from scratch, using $1/32$ as many target labels as that baseline point. Without any target oracle labels, HyperDn also reaches near-oracle PSNR on two unseen mixtures of seen noise types and on transfer from relatively cheap $96\times 96$ source images to $512\times 768$ targets. Together, these results show that expensive oracle supervision for hyperparameter prediction can be transferred from source to new target configurations, reducing the need to rebuild oracle labels for each new denoising configuration.
  </details>

- **[Rethinking the State Update Gate for Long-Sequence Recurrent 3D Reconstruction](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.16981)**  `arXiv:2605.16981`  
  _Kejun Ren, Lei Jin, Tianxin Huang, Lianming Xu, Li Wang_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Streaming 3D reconstruction under a strict constant-memory budget hinges on how the recurrent state is updated as the stream evolves. We profile TTT3R-style per-token gates across five benchmarks and discover a structural bottleneck: the gate is intrinsically bounded in magnitude (median $0.31$; never exceeding $0.6$) and nearly frame-invariant, yielding an effective memory horizon of only $\sim$3 frames per state token, which serves as the structural origin of long-sequence drift. We trace this to a missing axis: existing inference-time methods modulate updates only at the per-token, intra-frame level, while the orthogonal frame-level question of \emph{how strongly each frame should contribute to the state} has been treated as content-independent. We close this gap with a scalar frame-level gate $\alpha_t \in (0, 1]$ derived in closed form from frame-to-frame changes of internal features---a graded write weight, inspired by classical Simultaneous Localization and Mapping (SLAM) keyframe selection, that never discards a frame and requires no parameters, no training, and no extra forward pass. Across six benchmarks spanning camera pose, video depth, and 3D reconstruction at sequence lengths up to $4,661$ frames, our gate cuts ATE by $51\%$ on long TUM-RGBD pose sequences, reduces AbsRel by $13.0\%$ on Bonn video depth, and on KITTI long-sequence pose estimation surpasses both LongStream and Keyframe-VO in average ATE, while retaining strictly constant memory at zero training cost. Code is available atthis https URL.
  </details>

- **[DiRotQ: Rotation-Aware Quantization for 4-bit Diffusion Transformers](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.16732)**  `arXiv:2605.16732`  
  _Sayeh Sharify, Mahsa Salmani, Hesham Mostafa_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Diffusion Transformers (DiTs) achieve state-of-the-art image generation quality but incur substantial memory and computational costs at inference. While aggressive Post-Training Quantization (PTQ) to 4-bit precision offers significant efficiency gains, it typically results in severe quality degradation. Existing approaches, including smoothing-based methods, mixed-precision schemes, rotation techniques, and low-rank residual methods, partially mitigate this issue but still leave a noticeable gap to FP16/BF16 performance. In this work, we introduce DiRotQ, a W4A4 PTQ framework that mitigates this degradation through rotation-aware activation quantization. DiRotQ identifies a low-rank subspace capturing dominant activation variance via Principal Component Analysis (PCA), preserving coefficients in this subspace at higher precision while quantizing the remaining components to 4-bit. Activations are rotated into the PCA basis at inference time using calibration-derived orthogonal transformations, while the inverse rotation is fused into the layer weights offline. Combined with GPTQ-based weight quantization, DiRotQ achieves an FID of 15.9 and PSNR of 19.1 dB on PixArt over the MJHQ-30K dataset, outperforming the prior state-of-the-art SVDQuant (FID 18.9, PSNR 17.6) under the same INT W4A4 setting. Beyond standard metrics, we introduce a VLM-as-a-Judge evaluation protocol for diffusion model quantization, the first such evaluation in this setting, providing a more holistic assessment of perceptual quality and prompt alignment under aggressive compression. On the systems side, our Triton-based custom kernel enables efficient end-to-end inference, reducing memory usage of the 12B FLUX.1-dev model by 2.1x and achieving a 2.3x speedup over BF16 on an RTX 4090. On the RTX PRO 6000 with Blackwell architecture, DiRotQ achieves a 2.0x speedup and memory reduction over BF16 using NVFP4.
  </details>

- **[Beyond MMSE: Enhancing PnP Restoration with ProxiMAP](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.16396)**  `arXiv:2605.16396`  
  _Kenta Vert, Giacomo Meanti, Scott Pesme, Michael Arbel, Julien Mairal_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Plug-and-Play (PnP) methods for imaging inverse problems replace the proximal operator of the prior, a maximum a posteriori (MAP) denoiser, with a pretrained minimum mean squared error (MMSE) denoiser. MMSE estimates are oversmoothed, motivating recent work to target the MAP with diffusion-model scores. We show that MAP-targeting iterations converge to cartoon-like images with learned scores, but to realistic ones with the exact scores of a Gaussian mixture. The failure thus seems to come from score errors, and it only appears near convergence. We therefore propose ProxiMAP, an iterative MAP approximation that queries the denoiser at the residual noise level of the current iterate. This keeps the denoiser in-distribution and slows the iterations down before they reach the cartoon regime. On deblurring, super-resolution, inpainting, HDR and phase retrieval, replacing the MMSE denoiser with ProxiMAP in DPIR, DiffPIR and DAPS improves perceptual quality in most experiments, sometimes at the expense of PSNR. To make ProxiMAP cheaper, we also propose a one-step distillation and a hybrid schedule that applies it only at the last PnP iteration. In most cases, one or the other retains much of the improvement at a fraction of the cost.
  </details>

- **[Hide to See: Reasoning-prefix Masking for Visual-anchored Thinking in VLM Distillation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.11651)**  `arXiv:2605.11651`  
  _Seonghoon Yu, Dongjun Nam, Byung-Kwan Lee, Jeany Son_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Recent think-answer approaches in VLMs, such as Qwen3-VL-Thinking, boost reasoning performance by leveraging intermediate thinking steps before the final answer, but their computational cost becomes substantial, especially for larger VLMs. To distill such capabilities into compact think-answer VLMs, a primary objective is to improve the student's ability to utilize visual evidence throughout its reasoning trace, as long think-answer traces suffer from visual forgetting issues. To this end, we introduce a novel think-answer distillation framework that encourages the student to anchor its thinking on visual information by masking the student's salient reasoning prefixes. To compensate for such masked textual cues, the student is encouraged to rely more on visual evidence as an alternative source of information during distillation. Our masking strategies include: 1) token-wise salient reasoning-prefix masking, which masks high-influence reasoning prefixes selectively for each next-token prediction, and 2) self-paced masking budget scheduling, which gradually increases the masking scale according to distillation difficulty, measured by the discrepancy between teacher--student distributions. In the distillation phase, the student is guided by our salient reasoning-prefix mask, which blocks both future tokens and salient reasoning cues, in place of the standard causal mask used for auto-regressive language modeling. Experimental results show that our approach outperforms recent open-source VLMs, VLM distillation, and self-distillation methods on multimodal reasoning benchmarks, while further analyzes confirm enhanced visual utilization along the student thinking process.
  </details>

- **[PGID: Progressive Guided Inversion and Denoising for Robust Watermark Detection](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.09319)**  `arXiv:2605.09319`  
  _Minh Quoc Duong, Chun Tong Lei, Chun Pong Lau_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  With the proliferation of AI-generated images, digital watermarking has become an essential safeguard for protecting intellectual property and mitigating malicious exploitation. Recent works on semantic watermarking have enabled efficient copyright protection for diffusion models. However, the dependence of semantic watermarking on diffusion inversion for watermark detection creates a critical vulnerability. Imprint removal and forgery attacks exploit this weakness to produce deceptive results. Our analysis reveals that these attacks succeed by displacing watermarked latents into the unwatermarked region, while guiding unwatermarked latents into the watermarked region. Based on that, we propose Progressive Guided Inversion and Denoising (PGID), the first plug-and-play, training-free noise extraction framework designed to defend against both attack strategies. PGID effectively defends by projecting perturbed latents back to the region where they originally belong. The projection is achieved by eliminating intermediate latent deflections and mitigating adversarial perturbations through progressive inversion-denoising cycles. Comprehensive evaluations across multiple schemes demonstrate that PGID successfully restores detection reliability by recovering removed watermarks and identifying forged instances.
  </details>

- **[Local Intrinsic Dimension Unveils Hallucinations in Diffusion Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.05026)**  `arXiv:2605.05026`  
  _Bartlomiej Sobieski, Matthew Tivnan, Michał Jan Włodarczyk, Dawid Płudowski, Pengfei Jin, Przemyslaw Biecek, et al._
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Diffusion models are prone to generating structural hallucinations - samples that match the statistical properties of the training data yet defy underlying structural rules, resulting in anomalies like hands with more than five fingers. Recent research studied this failure mode from several viewpoints, offering partial explanations to their occurrence, such as mode interpolation. In this work, we propose a complementary perspective that treats hallucinations as instabilities on the model-induced manifold. We begin by showing that a hallucination filter based on such instabilities matches or exceeds the performance of the recently proposed temporal one. By tracing the source of these instabilities, we identify local intrinsic dimension (LID) as their primary driver and propose Intrinsic Quenching (IQ), a direct corrective mechanism that deflates it to alleviate hallucinations. IQ consistently outperforms standard hallucination reduction baselines across a wide array of benchmarks and offers a highly promising solution for enforcing anatomical consistency in downstream medical imaging tasks.
  </details>

- **[From Points to Targets: Online Foreground Affinity and Background Learning for Infrared Small Target Detection](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.00722)**  `arXiv:2605.00722`  
  _Qiancheng Zhou, Xiaodong Yue, Wenhua Zhang_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Infrared small-target detection must identify a few faint target pixels in extensive background clutter while keeping false alarms low. Under single-point supervision, each target has only one labeled foreground pixel with unknown spatial extent during training, whereas the detector must recover complete targets from the infrared image without any point guidance at inference. Existing methods typically reconstruct regional pseudo-labels from local cues or intermediate predictions, which can introduce boundary noise around blurry target edges.
